profile.campus: Piscataway, Middlesex County, New Jersey (QTS Piscataway 1 campus)

source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

profile.reading:
Per QTS's own site, Piscataway 1 sits on a 38-acre campus in the New York City metro region with 65+ MW of total critical power capacity; an expansion building (two-story, 50,000 sq ft, 15 MW) is noted, and the campus is LEED Gold certified with a 2MW rooftop solar field. QTS's page does not itself publish a specific street address beyond the general campus description; 101 Possumtown Road is this registry's previously recorded address for the facility.

QTS was founded in 2003 in Overland Park, Kansas, and was taken private in a roughly $10 billion Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust (BREIT)-led acquisition completed August 31, 2021, per Blackstone's own press release; QTS is no longer an independent SEC filer.

QTS positions itself as a "hyperscale-neutral" wholesale and colocation landlord, leasing built data center capacity to enterprise, cloud, and hyperscale tenants rather than operating its own end-user cloud service, a business model it shares with peers such as Digital Realty and CyrusOne. Since Blackstone completed its roughly $10 billion take-private acquisition in August 2021, QTS has continued expanding across multiple US metros rather than slowing development, including major campus filings and expansions in Phoenix (a 750MW, 375-acre Glendale campus acquired for $255.3 million in July 2022) and Dallas-Fort Worth (its two mega-scale Irving and Fort Worth campuses), consistent with the scale of buildout QTS has also pursued in Northern Virginia, Georgia, and Ohio, tracked elsewhere in this registry.

QTS was originally founded in 2003 in Overland Park, Kansas by Chad Williams, and grew through a mix of acquisitions and ground-up construction into a national wholesale/colocation platform before its 2013 IPO as a publicly traded REIT; that public period ended with the 2021 Blackstone take-private deal. QTS's current published portfolio language describes over 30 facilities across North America and Europe on its own site, while Wikipedia gives a somewhat different approximate figure of 28 locations across 16 US states plus two Netherlands sites (Eemshaven and Groningen), a discrepancy this registry notes rather than resolves in favor of either source.

reading.body:
The QTS Piscataway campus publishes 65 MW of IT capacity, making it the largest disclosed data center in New Jersey and accounting for roughly 69 percent of confirmed state capacity from operator spec pages.

New Jersey data center operators disclose power capacity selectively. Of 47 mapped facilities in the state, only two have published IT load figures. This opacity means the state's actual data center footprint is substantially unknown. What appears as Piscataway's dominance may reflect only QTS's willingness to publish, not the true distribution of power available to AI workloads across the region.

The 65 MW figure alone cannot reveal whether this campus suits dense AI training or general enterprise colocation. At 40 kW per rack, a typical density for GPU clusters, 65 MW supports roughly 1,625 racks. At 10 kW per rack, a common enterprise baseline, it supports 6,500. The operator publishes no cooling architecture, rack count, or power usage effectiveness metric, so the facility's actual suitability for compute-intensive workloads remains opaque. LEED Gold certification confirms environmental performance of the building envelope and systems, nothing about redundancy, uptime tier, or grid interconnection resilience.

Proximity to New York City and a 38-acre footprint with ongoing expansion signal regional infrastructure value. The gap between what the operator publishes and what AI infrastructure operators require for capacity planning demonstrates how incomplete public disclosure constrains visibility into the supply of dense compute real estate in high-density regions.
